title: The Afternoon Brief: Ratcliffe's Moscow visit raises questions about U.S.-Russia negotiations
dek: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25, prompting conflicting accounts about its purpose. Meanwhile, primary elections across multiple states reshaped the 2026 landscape, inflation data showed persistent headwinds for the Fed, and a major pancreatic cancer drug won FDA approval.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The substance and outcome of Ratcliffe's Moscow visit remain undisclosed despite reporting on its occurrence and stated purpose, leaving the administration's diplomatic strategy toward Russia unclear as economic data pressures the Federal Reserve.
bottom_line: Ratcliffe's Moscow trip and the administration's competing accounts of its purpose obscure what diplomatic concerns or intelligence prompted the unannounced mission and how Moscow responded. Primary elections extended the pattern of democratic socialist victories in high-profile Democratic races while GOP-backed candidates won in solidly Republican states; Alaska's unusual three-way general election will test ranked-choice voting dynamics. Persistent inflation above the Fed's target pressures rate-cut expectations ahead of Vice Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole address Friday. Watch for official clarification of Ratcliffe's Moscow meeting, the June 2028 trial date for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, and the outcome of the Secret Service investigation and Lindsay Clancy jury deliberations.
body: CIA Director John Ratcliffe's unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25 stands at the center of a day marked by fractured official messaging and incomplete disclosure. A C-17 transport plane carried Ratcliffe from Latvia, landing at Moscow's Vnukovo airport at approximately 07:04 GMT and departing before 17:00 GMT the same day, according to FlightRadar24 data reported by BBC News. Neither Washington nor Moscow initially disclosed the purpose or who Ratcliffe met. Subsequent reporting by the Wall Street Journal and CBS News, cited by the Guardian, characterized the trip as a warning to Russia against attacking NATO member states. President Trump later described it as "semi-routine" and denied it was motivated by concerns about Russian plans to test NATO resolve or by negotiations over Iran sanctions. The gap between the trip's occurrence and the competing accounts of its substance leaves the diplomatic intent unconfirmed. Ukraine paused drone strikes during Ratcliffe's presence in Moscow and resumed attacks hours after his departure, according to the desk's reporting.

Primary elections in multiple states on August 25 and 26 extended patterns from earlier in the 2026 cycle. N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a 31-year-old democratic socialist and member of the Chickasaw Nation, won the Oklahoma Democratic Senate primary runoff with 70 percent of the vote, defeating attorney and minister Jim Priest. Thomas spent $57,000 to Priest's $315,000, continuing a string of democratic socialist primary victories despite Oklahoma's status as a solidly Republican state that President Trump won by 34 points in 2024. She will face Republican Rep. Kevin Hern in November. Mike Mazzei, a former Oklahoma state senator backed by President Trump, defeated Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the Republican gubernatorial runoff, securing the GOP nomination and positioning himself as the heavy favorite in the general election. In Georgia's 13th Congressional District, Everton Blair Jr., former chair of the Gwinnett County School Board, defeated Marcye Scott in Tuesday's special election runoff to serve the remaining few months of Rep. David Scott's term. In Alaska, the all-party primary advanced incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, Republican Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (a retired teacher), and Democrat Mary Peltola to the November general election, which will use ranked-choice voting. Federal prosecutors are investigating whether Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters; a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to his campaign, per NBC News.

Economic data released Wednesday showed persistent inflation above the Federal Reserve's target. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, remained flat at 3.7% annually in July, matching June and exceeding the 3.6% forecast. Core PCE, excluding energy and food, rose to 3.3%, also above the 3.2% forecast and matching June. Both measures remain 1.7 percentage points above the Fed's 2% target. The readings come ahead of Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Warsh's Jackson Hole address Friday, which may signal the Fed's next move on interest rates.

The FDA approved daraxonrasib (Rasonque), made by Revolution Medicines, on Wednesday for advanced pancreatic cancer. In a 500-patient late-stage trial, median survival reached 13.2 months compared to 6.6 to 6.7 months on chemotherapy. The drug targets KRAS mutations present in over 90 percent of pancreatic tumors. FDA Oncology Center of Excellence Director Angelo de Claro characterized the approval as reflecting "unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need." The agency approved the drug six months ahead of its regulatory deadline.

A military judge set June 5, 2028, as the trial date for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, alleged architect of the September 11 attacks, rejecting prosecutors' proposed January 2027 start date. Air Force Lt. Col. Michael Schrama allowed approximately 18 additional months for procedural matters. Mohammed, held at Guantanamo Bay since 2006 and charged in 2008, will be prosecuted alongside Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, and Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi on charges of conspiring in the 2001 attacks. Closing arguments are underway in the trial of Lindsay Clancy in Massachusetts, with a judge clearing the way for jurors to consider a manslaughter charge. The case centers on the deaths of three children and raises questions about postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency affecting 1 to 2 per 1,000 women after delivery.

Three non-law enforcement personnel in the Secret Service's communications office were placed on administrative leave Tuesday pending investigation by the Office of Professional Responsibility. The three officials included Secret Service communications chief Anthony Guglielmi. The agency did not disclose the nature of the alleged misconduct. The suspension coincides with elevated Iranian threats against Trump family members.
